title: Heuristic catalogue for runtime quirks and customer hacks — compact synthesis
content:
TL;DR
A compact, pragmatic catalogue of the most common runtime quirks customers report and the ad-hoc "hacks" they deploy to keep production systems running. Goal is to move a subset of these hacks into low-risk product patches or documented runbook items. This doc is a working synthesis from CS triage notes (Q3–Q4 2026), three postmortems, and 14 customer interviews.

Context and scope
- Source: field notes + support tickets + 1:1s with 7 enterprise customers (FinCo, HealthML, EduApp, ChatOps Inc., RetailAi) collected Aug–Oct 2026.
- Focus: runtime-level issues that manifest in production inference (latency spikes, token regressions, KV cache anomalies, batching inefficiencies). Not covering UI/console UX.
- Audience: eng-serving-runtime, product-hosted-api, solutions-eng.

Top recurring runtime quirks (ranked by frequency & customer pain)
1) KV cache warmup inconsistency
   - Symptom: first N requests after a cold-start or model switch have weird latency and sometimes truncated completions. Customers see increased token use as they re-send prompts.
   - Customer hack: clients pre-send short seeded prompts ("prime requests") during warmup window to populate the cache manually.
   - Impact: medium latency cost + customer churn risk on model-switch features.
2) Silent fallback to CPU variant under load
   - Symptom: traffic bursts trigger fallback to a lower-throughput variant; not always surfaced as an event to the customer.
   - Customer hack: customers pin a low-QPS 'test' route which they trigger on scale events; treat it as a canary.
   - Impact: high user-visible latency and cost unpredictability.
3) Prefix-caching mismatch with streaming responses
   - Symptom: when streaming is enabled, prefix cache hit rates drop vs non-streaming; leads to higher token charge and latency for repeated prompts.
   - Customer hack: customer-side deduping — they detect repeated prefixes client-side and short-circuit requests to their own cache.
   - Impact: cost increase for high-repetition workloads (chatbots with short-system prompts).
4) Tokenization divergence across quantized variants
   - Symptom: slightly different tokenization boundaries for quantized models cause hallucinated token counts or misaligned reranking heuristics.
   - Customer hack: conservative overruns (asking for +20 tokens buffer) or local tokenization checks before sending.
   - Impact: low-latency correctness edgecases, medium cost when buffers used aggressively.

Representative customer quotes (anonymized)
- "We spun up a warmup job that pings your endpoint every hour — it costs us but reduced surprises." — FinCo
- "Our SREs treat Redwood like a two-tier system: golden lane + fallback lane. We need better signals when a lane changes." — ChatOps Inc.
- "Streaming made things worse for us on token costs; we had to implement our own prefix cache in front of the API." — EduApp

Quick wins (low engineering effort, high customer value)
- Expose a clear 'fallback' webhook/event (emit when requests are routed off preferred variant) — Owner: eng-serving-runtime (JIRA INF-987) — 3–5 days
- 'Warmup mode' helper API: lightweight optional endpoint that accepts an array of seed prompts and returns warmup heartbeat with expected KV state summary — Owner: product-hosted-api + eng-serving-runtime (RFC) — 2 sprints to spec/prototype
- Streaming + prefix-cache diagnostic flag (return cache hit metadata header) — Owner: observability team — 1 sprint

Medium scope proposals (worth grooming into epics)
- Runtime-aware prefix caching: stronger guarantees for cache hits when streaming enabled; may require serialized cache writes or streaming-aware cache keys. Risk: nontrivial kernel/runtime changes.
- Fallback transparency + routing policy improvements: allow customers to opt into strict-capacity enforcement (reject rather than fallback) per-route.

Customer-level mitigations and temporary runbook items (for CS/solutions-eng)
- Template: warmup-job (cron) + sample seed list per customer profile (chatbot, summarizer, embedding-heavy). Ship in Solutions Playbook.
- Suggested alerting: SLO breach + routing-change event within 5 minutes -> notify oncall + customer primary.
- Documentation snippet: how to detect tokenization divergence and a quick local test (token counts for inputs + expected outputs on both float/quantized variants).

Prioritization rationale (short)
- Highest immediate value: visibility into fallback events (reduces surprise + enables SRE automation).
- Next: warmup-mode API (reduces ad-hoc customer warmup jobs and repeated tokens).
- Longer-term: streaming-aware cache changes and tokenization normalization across variants.

Open questions and unknowns
- How often do customers trigger their manual warmup (cron frequency) and what's the typical cost? Need instrumentation query across accounts.
- Are there predictable traffic shape thresholds where fallback happens? Need sample traces from infra for 10 incidents.
- Feasibility of returning lightweight KV cache diagnostics without leaking model internals or PII. Security review required.

Suggested next steps (owner and timelines)
1) eng-observability: add header/metric for routing variant and cache-hit boolean to prod endpoints — P0 probe; 2 weeks.
2) CS + Solutions: roll out warmup-job playbook to top 12 enterprise accounts and collect feedback — 2 weeks.
3) product + serving-runtime: draft RFC for 'warmup-mode' API + fallback opt-in flags — write in next sprint (start in 1 week).

Appendix: quick checklist for CS conversations
- Ask whether customer uses streaming + short system prompts (yes/no)
- Do they run a warmup cron? If yes, capture cadence and sample prompt list
- Ask whether they saw silent latency increases (no explicit error) or explicit failed requests
- Offer 'routing transparency' beta (once header/metric exists) and capture acceptance

Notes to self
- Collate infra traces (INF-logs) for incidents tagged "fallback" between 2026-07 and 2026-10.
- Coordinate with security for safe KV diagnostic surface.
- Follow up with Marco and Emily for a trimmed 1-pager to send to product leadership.

End of doc.
